column2: On the authority of Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:

“Islam has been built upon five: testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing the prayer, giving the zakāh, pilgrimage to the House, and fasting Ramaḍān.” Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.
His words, “Islam has been built upon five”, show the great importance of these five and that Islam is built upon them. It is a comparison of something abstract to a physical building:

just as a physical building stands only on its pillars, Islam likewise stands only on these five. These five alone are mentioned because they are the foundation for everything else, and everything besides them is subordinate to them.

Al-Nawawī cited this hadith after the hadith of Jibrīl, which also contains these five, because this hadith makes clear the importance of these five and that they are the foundation on which Islam is built; so it contains a meaning beyond what came in the hadith of Jibrīl.
Of these five pillars on which Islam is built, the first is the two testimonies. They are the foundation of foundations, and the remaining pillars and everything else follow them.

These pillars and other deeds are of no benefit if they are not built on these two testimonies. The two are inseparable: the testimony that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah must accompany the testimony that there is no god but Allah.

The testimony that there is no god but Allah requires that none be worshipped except Allah, and the testimony that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah requires that worship be in accordance with what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ brought.
These are two principles that are indispensable for the acceptance of any deed a person does: his sincerity must be purely for Allah alone, and his following purely of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
The ḥāfiẓ [Ibn Ḥajar] said in al-Fatḥ (1/50): “If it is said: Why are belief in the prophets and the angels and the other things contained in the question of Jibrīl (peace be upon him) not mentioned?

The answer is that what is meant by the testimony is believing the Messenger in what he brought, which necessarily entails all the beliefs mentioned. Al-Ismāʿīlī said, in substance: It is a case of calling a thing by part of it,
as when you say, ‘I recited al-Ḥamd’, meaning the whole of al-Fātiḥah; likewise you might say, ‘I testified to the messengership of Muḥammad’, meaning everything mentioned. And Allah knows best.”

The most important of the five pillars of Islam after the two testimonies is the prayer. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ described it as the central pillar of Islam, as in the hadith in which he ﷺ counselled Muʿādh ibn Jabal,

which is the twenty-ninth hadith of this Forty. He also informed us that it is the last thing of the religion to be lost and the first thing for which the servant will be called to account on the Day of Resurrection
(see al-Silsilah al-Ṣaḥīḥah by al-Albānī, 1739, 1358, 1748), and that by it the Muslim is distinguished from the disbeliever (reported by Muslim, 134). Establishing it takes two forms:

one obligatory, which is performing it with the minimum that fulfils the obligation and discharges one's duty; and one recommended, which is completing and perfecting it by doing everything that is recommended in it.
Zakāh is the companion of prayer in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

“But if they repent, establish the prayer and give the zakāh, then let them go on their way” [al-Tawbah 9:5]; and the Exalted says: “But if they repent, establish the prayer and give the zakāh, then they are your brothers in religion” [al-Tawbah 9:11];

and the Exalted says: “And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion, inclining to truth, and to establish the prayer and give the zakāh; and that is the upright religion” [al-Bayyinah 98:5]. It is a financial act of worship whose benefit extends to others. Allah has made it obligatory on the wealth of the rich in a way that benefits the poor and does not harm the rich,
because it is a small portion of much wealth.
Fasting Ramaḍān is a bodily act of worship, and it is a secret between the servant and his Lord which none but Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, sees,
because some people may not be fasting in Ramaḍān while others think they are fasting, and a person may be observing a voluntary fast while others think he is not.

That is why the authentic hadith states that a person is recompensed for his deeds, a good deed tenfold, up to seven hundred times, and that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “Except fasting, for it is Mine, and I Myself shall reward it.” Reported by al-Bukhārī (1894)

and Muslim (164), that is, without measure. All deeds are for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “Say: Indeed, my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds. He has no partner; this I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims” [al-Anʿām 6:162–163].
Fasting is singled out in this hadith as being for Allah only because this act of worship is hidden and none sees it but Allah.

Ḥajj to the Sacred House of Allah is a financial and bodily act of worship, which Allah has made obligatory once in a lifetime. The Prophet ﷺ explained its virtue, saying: “Whoever performs Ḥajj to this House without obscenity or wrongdoing returns as on the day his mother bore him.” Reported by al-Bukhārī (1820)
and Muslim (1350). And he ﷺ said: “One ʿUmrah to the next is an expiation for what is between them, and an accepted Ḥajj (ḥajj mabrūr) has no reward but Paradise.” Reported by Muslim (1349).

In this hadith, with this wording, Ḥajj is mentioned before fasting. It is with this wording that al-Bukhārī cited it at the beginning of the Book of Faith in his Ṣaḥīḥ, and he based the arrangement of his book al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaḥīḥ on it, placing the Book of Ḥajj before the Book of Fasting.

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (19) the hadith appears both with fasting before Ḥajj and with Ḥajj before fasting. In the first route, Ibn ʿUmar states explicitly that what he heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was fasting before Ḥajj.
Accordingly, putting Ḥajj before fasting in some narrations comes from some narrators' handling of the wording and from narration by meaning.

Its wording in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Ibn ʿUmar, from the Prophet ﷺ, is: “Islam has been built upon five: on Allah being worshipped alone, establishing the prayer, giving the zakāh, fasting Ramaḍān, and Ḥajj.” A man said: “Ḥajj and fasting Ramaḍān?” He said: “No:
fasting Ramaḍān and Ḥajj. That is how I heard it from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.”

These five pillars are listed in the hadith in order of their importance. It begins with the two testimonies, which are the foundation of every deed by which one seeks nearness to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic;
then the prayer, which is repeated five times in a day and night and is a firm bond between the servant and his Lord; then zakāh, which becomes due on wealth once a year has passed over it,

since its benefit extends to others; then fasting, which is obligatory for one month in the year and is a bodily act of worship whose benefit does not extend to others; and then Ḥajj, which is obligatory only once in a lifetime.
It is reported in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim that Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both) narrated the hadith when a man asked him, saying: Will you not go out on military expeditions?

He then related the hadith. This indicates that jihād is not one of the pillars of Islam, because these five are constantly binding on every legally responsible person, unlike jihād, which is a communal obligation (farḍ kifāyah) and is not required at all times.
These five are of great importance, since Islam is built upon them.
Abstract matters may be compared to physical ones to fix them firmly in the mind.
One should begin with what is most important, then with what is next in importance.
The two testimonies are a foundation in themselves and a foundation for everything else; no deed is accepted unless it is built upon them.
The prayer takes precedence over other deeds,
because it is a firm bond between the servant and his Lord.
